blocks.content: Think about a wall socket. It does not care whether you plug in a lamp, a phone charger, or a blender. It just exposes a standard shape, and any device with the right plug can use it. The socket has no idea what is on the other end.

That is the entire idea behind hexagonal architecture. Your business logic is the socket. It defines a standard shape it is willing to talk through, and it genuinely does not care whether the thing plugged into it is a real Postgres database, an in memory fake used in tests, or a message queue that has not been built yet.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308206-97500577.png
blocks.alt: HTTP adapter and Postgres adapter and queue adapter all plugging into a central order core

blocks.content: This pattern is also called ports and adapters, which is honestly the more useful name. The word hexagonal just refers to the shape people usually draw the core as, a hexagon with several sides, one for each place the core talks to the outside world. The shape does not matter. What matters is the core sits in the middle, isolated, and everything external plugs into it through a defined boundary.
1. Introduction

Most business logic ends up quietly welded to whatever database, framework, or API client the team happened to pick on day one. You import the Postgres client directly into your order processing function. You call the payment provider SDK straight from inside your checkout logic. It works, right up until you need to test that logic without hitting a real database, or you need to swap providers, or you need to expose the same logic through a second interface like a CLI or an internal admin tool.

Hexagonal architecture is a way of structuring code so that never has to happen. The core business rules live in one place, untouched by the specifics of any database or framework, and everything external talks to that core through a small set of defined interfaces.
1.1 The Core Idea

The business logic sits in the center. It knows nothing about HTTP, nothing about SQL, nothing about which message broker you use. It only knows the rules of the domain: an order can be placed, a payment can be marked as captured, a user can be verified.

["The core defines what it needs from the outside world as an interface, called a port.","Anything outside the core, a database, a queue, an external API, plugs into that port through an adapter.","The core never imports an adapter directly. It only ever talks to the port."]
items: The core defines what it needs from the outside world as an interface, called a port.
Anything outside the core, a database, a queue, an external API, plugs into that port through an adapter.
The core never imports an adapter directly. It only ever talks to the port.

blocks.title: Same idea, different names
blocks.content: You will see this pattern called hexagonal architecture, ports and adapters, and sometimes just clean architecture in blog posts that blur the distinctions a bit. The core mechanics are the same everywhere: isolate the domain, define boundaries as interfaces, plug in implementations from outside.
1.2 Where The Name Comes From

Alistair Cockburn coined this pattern in the early 2000s, and he drew the core as a hexagon in his original diagrams. Not because six sides mean anything specific, but because a hexagon has enough sides to show multiple ports without looking like a cramped rectangle.
The hexagon has nothing to do with the number six. It is just a shape with enough room to draw several ports around a core without them overlapping.
Ignore the hexagon. Focus on what it represents: a core with a boundary, and things plugging into that boundary from every direction, none of them privileged over the others.
2. Why Hexagonal Architecture Matters
None of this is architecture for its own sake. Each piece solves a specific, recurring pain that shows up once a codebase grows past a toy project.
2.1 Swappable Infrastructure

If your business logic only talks to a port, the concrete adapter behind that port becomes a implementation detail. Swap Postgres for DynamoDB. Swap a REST call to a payment provider for a different provider entirely. As long as the new adapter satisfies the same port, the core does not change at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308208-802104189.png
blocks.alt: Order core talking to a repository port, with a Postgres adapter swapped for an in memory adapter

blocks.content: 2.2 Testability Without A Real Database

This is the big one in practice. Because the core depends on a port, not on Postgres itself, your tests can hand the core a fake adapter, usually a small in memory implementation, instead of standing up a real database.

["Tests run in milliseconds instead of seconds, because there is no real connection, no real disk, no real network hop.","Tests are deterministic. A fake in memory map does not have connection pool limits or flaky network blips.","You test the business rule, not the database driver."]
items: Tests run in milliseconds instead of seconds, because there is no real connection, no real disk, no real network hop.
Tests are deterministic. A fake in memory map does not have connection pool limits or flaky network blips.
You test the business rule, not the database driver.

blocks.title: This does not replace integration tests
blocks.content: You still want a handful of tests that run the real Postgres adapter against a real database, to confirm the adapter itself actually satisfies the contract correctly. Fakes test your logic. Integration tests confirm your adapters are honest.
2.3 Adding New Delivery Mechanisms Without Touching The Core
blocks.text: 2.3 Adding New Delivery Mechanisms Without Touching The Core

blocks.content: Say your order logic currently only runs behind an HTTP API. Six months later, ops wants a CLI tool to replay failed orders manually. In a tangled codebase, that means copying logic or awkwardly reaching into HTTP handler functions.

With hexagonal architecture, the CLI is just another adapter driving the same core. It calls the same core functions the HTTP handler calls. The core never finds out it is being invoked from a terminal instead of a web request.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308209-426528421.png
blocks.alt: A CLI adapter and an HTTP adapter both calling into the same order core

blocks.content: 3. Hexagonal Architecture Versus Layered Architecture

If you have worked in a typical layered codebase, controller calls service, service calls repository, repository calls database, this might sound familiar. It is related, but the direction of dependency is genuinely different, and that difference is the whole point.
3.1 How Layered Architecture Works
Layered architecture stacks responsibilities top to bottom. The UI layer calls the business layer, the business layer calls the data layer, and the data layer talks to the actual database.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308210-806936435.png
blocks.alt: UI layer calling business layer calling data layer calling the database, stacked top to bottom

blocks.content: This is fine, and plenty of successful systems are built this way. But notice that the business layer usually still depends downward, on a data layer that is itself tied to a specific database technology. Swapping databases means touching the data layer, and often the business layer notices too, because query shapes and transaction handling leak upward.
3.2 Where Hexagonal Architecture Differs

Hexagonal architecture puts the core in the middle instead of at the top of a stack. Everything else, the database, the HTTP layer, the queue, sits at the edges and depends on the core, not the other way around.

["Layered architecture: fixed direction, top to bottom, business logic depends on the data layer beneath it.","Hexagonal architecture: the core is the center, everything else is replaceable at the edges, and dependencies point inward toward the core."]
items: Layered architecture: fixed direction, top to bottom, business logic depends on the data layer beneath it.
Hexagonal architecture: the core is the center, everything else is replaceable at the edges, and dependencies point inward toward the core.

blocks.content: 3.3 Dependencies Always Point Inward

This is the rule that actually matters day to day. The Postgres adapter depends on the core, because it implements a port the core defined. The core never imports the Postgres adapter. If you trace every arrow in the codebase, they should all point toward the center.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308210-423731781.png
blocks.alt: HTTP adapter, Postgres adapter, and queue adapter, all with arrows pointing inward toward the core

blocks.title: A quick test for your own codebase
blocks.content: Open your core domain module. If it has an import statement referencing a specific database driver, an HTTP framework, or a specific queue client, your dependencies are pointing the wrong way. The core should only ever import its own ports.
4. Ports And Adapters
These two words carry the whole pattern, so it is worth being precise about what each one actually is.
4.1 Ports: Interfaces The Core Defines

A port is an interface, owned by the core, describing what the core needs from the outside world, without saying anything about how that need gets fulfilled. An OrderRepository port might declare a save method and a find by id method. It says nothing about SQL, connections, or tables.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308211-469043714.png
blocks.alt: Order core defining a repository interface with a save order method and a find by id method

blocks.content: 4.2 Adapters: Concrete Implementations

An adapter is the concrete class that actually implements a port. A Postgres adapter implements the OrderRepository port by running real SQL. An in memory adapter implements the exact same port by pushing objects into a plain map. Both satisfy the same contract, so the core cannot tell them apart.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308212-914435744.png
blocks.alt: One repository port with three different adapters plugging into it, Postgres, Mongo, and in memory

blocks.content: 4.3 Driving Ports And Driven Ports

Not every port faces the same direction. A driving port, sometimes called a primary port, is how something outside calls into the core, like an HTTP handler invoking a use case. A driven port, sometimes called a secondary port, is how the core calls out to something it needs, like a database or a payment gateway.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308212-526876221.png
blocks.alt: HTTP adapter driving the core, and the core driving a DB adapter through a secondary port

blocks.title: Same word, opposite direction of the arrow
blocks.content: Driving ports get called by adapters. Driven ports get implemented by adapters. It is easy to mix these up at first, so when in doubt, ask who is calling whom.
5. Worked Example: An Order Service
Concepts are easier to hold onto with a concrete example. Here is a small order service built the hexagonal way.
5.1 The Core Domain Logic

The OrderService class holds the actual business rule: an order can be marked as paid, but only if it exists. It depends on an OrderRepository, but only through the port, never through a specific database client.
5.2 The OrderRepository Port
The port is just an interface. It says nothing about SQL, connections, or tables, only what the core needs: a way to save an order, and a way to find one by id.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308212-233129900.png
blocks.alt: HTTP API calling order core, order core calling repository port, port calling Postgres adapter

blocks.content: 5.3 The Postgres Adapter

In production, this port gets satisfied by an adapter that actually talks to Postgres. Nothing about this class is special to the core, it just needs to honor the same method signatures the port declares.
5.4 The In Memory Fake Adapter For Tests
blocks.text: 5.4 The In Memory Fake Adapter For Tests

blocks.content: For tests, a second adapter satisfies the exact same port using nothing more than a plain map. No network, no real database, no setup and teardown of test data in a container.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396308213-220623317.png
blocks.alt: Unit test calling order core, order core calling fake adapter, fake adapter backed by an in memory map

blocks.title: Keep the fake honest
blocks.content: A fake adapter is only useful if it behaves like the real one for the cases you care about. If save is supposed to overwrite an existing order, make sure the fake actually overwrites instead of silently keeping two copies.
6.4 Wiring The Fake Into A Test
blocks.text: 6.4 Wiring The Fake Into A Test

blocks.content: No database container spun up, no network call, no cleanup step between tests. Just the core logic and a fake standing in for the port.
7. Multiple Adapters Driving The Same Core
blocks.text: 7. Multiple Adapters Driving The Same Core

blocks.content: Ports work in both directions. Just as the core can be handed different adapters for the same driven port, different driving adapters can call into the exact same core logic.
7.1 A CLI Adapter And An HTTP Adapter
blocks.text: 7.1 A CLI Adapter And An HTTP Adapter

blocks.content: An HTTP handler parses a request body, extracts an order id, and calls orderService.markAsPaid. A CLI command parses a command line argument, extracts the same order id, and calls the exact same orderService.markAsPaid. Neither adapter knows the other exists, and the core does not know or care which one called it.

blocks.title: Same core, two front doors
blocks.text: A support engineer running "node cli.js mark-paid order-1" from a terminal triggers the identical business rule as a customer clicking pay in the app. Both paths go through OrderService.markAsPaid. Only the adapter at the edge changes.

blocks.content: 8. The Practical Cost
None of this is free. Hexagonal architecture trades simplicity for flexibility, and that trade only pays off if you actually need the flexibility.
8.1 More Upfront Interfaces And Indirection

Writing directly against a database client is fewer files and fewer decisions. Define a port, write an interface, write at least one adapter, wire it all together with some form of dependency injection, and you have added several layers of indirection before you have shipped a single feature.

8.2 When It Is Not Worth It
blocks.text: 8.2 When It Is Not Worth It

blocks.content: A small internal tool with one client, one database, and no plans to ever swap either, does not need this. You would be paying the cost of ports and adapters for a flexibility you will never use.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396311130-386771366.png
blocks.alt: Simple CRUD app skipping hexagonal architecture, complex domain using hexagonal architecture

blocks.title: A rough rule of thumb
blocks.content: Reach for hexagonal architecture when the domain logic is complex enough to be worth protecting, or when you already know you need to swap infrastructure or add a second interface. Skip it for a thin CRUD wrapper around a single table.
9. The Interview Angle
This pattern comes up a lot in system design interviews, usually phrased as some version of how do you keep business logic testable while keeping infrastructure swappable.
9.1 How To Answer The Testability Question
blocks.text: 9.1 How To Answer The Testability Question

blocks.content: Say that the core domain logic should depend on interfaces it defines itself, ports, rather than on concrete infrastructure. Then real implementations, adapters, get injected at the edges. In tests, you inject a fake adapter instead of a real database, so tests run fast and stay deterministic.
9.2 Follow Up Questions To Expect

["How is this different from a plain layered architecture? Point at the direction of dependencies, everything points inward toward the core instead of stacking top to bottom.","Where do you draw the line for a port? Anything the core needs from outside its own domain rules, persistence, external APIs, messaging.","What is the cost? More interfaces and indirection than writing directly against a client, and it is not worth it for simple CRUD systems."]
items: How is this different from a plain layered architecture? Point at the direction of dependencies, everything points inward toward the core instead of stacking top to bottom.
Where do you draw the line for a port? Anything the core needs from outside its own domain rules, persistence, external APIs, messaging.
What is the cost? More interfaces and indirection than writing directly against a client, and it is not worth it for simple CRUD systems.

blocks.content: 10. Summary
10.1 When Hexagonal Architecture Is Worth It
blocks.text: 10.1 When Hexagonal Architecture Is Worth It

blocks.content: Reach for it when your domain logic is complex enough to deserve protecting from infrastructure churn, when you know you will need to swap a database or a provider down the line, or when the same logic needs to be driven from more than one entry point, like an API and a CLI.

blocks.title: Recap
blocks.text: Hexagonal architecture puts business logic in the center and isolates it from the outside world through ports, interfaces the core defines, and adapters, concrete implementations that plug into those ports. Unlike layered architecture, where dependencies point downward through fixed layers, hexagonal architecture keeps every dependency pointing inward toward the core. The payoff is a core you can test with fakes and infrastructure you can swap without touching business rules, at the cost of writing more interfaces and indirection than calling a database client directly.
